doc.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: St. Louis Blues, Tea for Two and tunes pianists claim
summary: Tunes like St. Louis Blues and Tea for Two attract signature versions from many pianists; Tommy Flanagan on structure and changes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: By the way, “St. Louis Blues” has been one of those tunes that Earl Hines had the wonderful rendition of that tune, and one of those tunes that became a tour de force for piano players you know. Even Willie “The Lion” Smith, the great stride piano player, he said that the greatest tune ever written was the “St. Louis Blues.” Tommy Flanagan even recorded the “St. Louis Blues.” So that’s one of those tunes, like another one for example is “Tea for Two” — that all the great piano players, they came up with a signed version of “Tea for Two.” There is the Fats Waller version, the Art Tatum version, the Bud Powell version, the Nat King Cole version, the Oscar Peterson version. It’s one of those tunes that somehow piano players felt they had to say their own thing through that tune.
I love that kind of composition that just has something that attracts it. When I play that tune I love the — I guess it’s the first 8 bars going into the second 8, that harmonic transition is so hip.

Yeah. Tommy Flanagan was once interviewed and said that what attracts him in a song is the structure of the tune and the chords. Because there is a way of using the harmony that when you play the tune you just feel like blowing on those chords, on those changes, it’s the most exciting thing to do. So there are tunes that are constructed in a certain way, that they are just an invitation to jazz improvisation you know.
